title: The Golden Calf and Broken Tablets
overview: While Moses is on the mountain receiving God's laws, the people make a golden calf to worship, and the chapter follows what comes next: God's anger, Moses' pleading, a violent punishment, and an uneasy way forward.

parts.label: The people demand a god (vv. 1-6)
parts.note: With Moses gone for weeks, the people pressed Aaron for a visible god, and he cast a calf from their gold and announced a feast to the LORD. Many scholars think the calf was meant as an image of Israel's own God, since bull figures stood for divine strength in Egypt and Canaan, but making it still broke the recent command against images.

parts.label: Moses pleads for them (vv. 7-14)
parts.note: God threatens to destroy the people and build a new nation from Moses, but Moses argues this would let Egypt think God meant them harm and would break the promises to Abraham, Isaac and Israel (another name for Jacob). The text says the LORD relented, and readers differ on how to understand that.

parts.label: Tablets smashed, calf destroyed (vv. 15-20)
parts.note: The text says Moses threw down and broke the stone tablets God had written on because his anger burned; many interpreters also see the act as a sign that the people had broken their agreement with God. He then burned the calf, ground it to powder and made the people drink it in water, which at least showed the idol to be worthless, though what else the drinking meant is uncertain.

parts.label: Aaron's excuse (vv. 21-24)
parts.note: Aaron blames the people's bent toward evil and claims he just threw gold into the fire and the calf came out. The story has already told us he shaped it himself, so the reader can see the excuse does not hold up.

parts.label: The Levites' killing (vv. 25-29)
parts.note: Moses calls those loyal to the LORD, and the men of the tribe of Levi go through the camp killing about three thousand people, including relatives and neighbors. The text presents this as the day the Levites were set apart for God's service, and it is a brutal scene that the story does not soften.

parts.label: Moses offers himself (vv. 30-35)
parts.note: Moses asks God to forgive the people or else erase his own name from God's book, an image likely drawn from a register of the living, but God says those who sinned will answer for it and sends them on with an angel, followed by a plague. Christians have often read Moses' offer as pointing ahead to Jesus giving himself for others.

disagreement: Christians differ on what it means that the LORD relented after Moses prayed: whether prayer truly changed God's course, or whether God's purpose was fixed and the threat served to draw out Moses' plea.
think: When a leader or a hope seems to go silent for a long time, what do people tend to reach for to fill the gap?
